lab.title: Lab Challenges
lab.subtitle: Behold, the mighty botnets!
lab.description: This year's CTF theme focuses on botnet development, challenging participants to explore how botnets are designed, built, and operated in a controlled environment. By understanding the inner workings of botnets, their communication mechanisms, and attack strategies, participants will gain valuable insights into how these threats function in the real world. The ultimate goal is to bridge offensive and defensive security knowledge, equipping defenders with the skills and understanding needed to better detect, analyze, mitigate, and defend against botnet threats.

questions.title: Botnet Challenge
questions.description:
Participants are challenged to develop and deploy a botnet inspired by existing botnets such as Mirai or Satori. The botnet should demonstrate key characteristics of real-world botnet architectures, including command-and-control (C2) communication, device management, and coordinated operations.

Participants may use publicly disclosed CVEs to demonstrate how vulnerable systems can be compromised within the designated CTF environment. The objective is to understand how botnets are constructed and operate, providing defensive teams with a realistic adversarial scenario to investigate and defend against.

Once development is complete, the submitted botnet will be examined by the referees and defensive teams, who will evaluate its behavior, architecture, and security implications.

hero.headline: Unknown Binary. Zero Signatures. Find the Threat.
hero.description: An unrecognized binary was recovered from an internal server. Code-signing checks, AV engines, and known-hash databases all returned clean. Threat intelligence suggests APT involvement. You are the analyst on call. Decompile it. Map the logic. Identify the vulnerability.

categories.name: Triage
categories.description: Identify file format, architecture, compiler artifacts, and packer signatures before deeper analysis.

categories.name: Deobfuscation
categories.description: Strip packing layers, decode encrypted strings, and reconstruct the original code flow.

categories.name: Code Mapping
categories.description: Reconstruct function boundaries, call graphs, and data structures from raw disassembly.

categories.name: Behavioral Analysis
categories.description: Run the binary in a controlled sandbox and trace API calls, file I/O, registry changes, and network activity.

categories.name: C2 Analysis
categories.description: Identify command-and-control channels, decode beaconing protocols, and extract remote endpoints.

categories.name: Vuln Identification
categories.description: Locate the specific code path — backdoor, exploit primitive, or logic flaw — that an attacker leverages.

schedule.event: Triage and initial fingerprinting of recovered binary
Static analysis — full code reconstruction
Dynamic analysis — controlled sandbox execution
Vulnerability identification and exploitation path mapping
IOC extraction and incident report submission

faq.a: The binary uses a custom packer, stripped symbols, and no network signatures. It was compiled specifically to evade signature-based detection. Manual analysis is the only reliable path.

faq.q: Is it safe to run the binary?
faq.a: Only inside the isolated lab VM with no network access. The binary has active network callbacks. Running it on a live system risks lateral movement.

faq.q: What is the IOC flag format?
faq.a: Each objective reveals an Indicator of Compromise wrapped in IOC{...}. These are real artifacts extracted from the binary — C2 addresses, hardcoded keys, function hashes.

faq.q: What tools are available in the lab?
faq.a: The lab VM includes Ghidra, Binary Ninja, x64dbg, Wireshark, Process Monitor, FLOSS, Cutter, and a Python 3 environment with pwntools and capstone.

lab.title: Mission Objectives
lab.subtitle: CLASSIFICATION: INTERNAL — Security Operations Use Only
lab.description: An unrecognized 64-bit PE binary (SHA-256: redacted) was recovered from C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\svchost32.exe on a finance workstation. It has been present for an estimated 14 days. No AV vendor currently detects it. Work through each objective in order. Do not execute the binary outside the provided sandbox VM. Submit each IOC flag as you find it.

questions.title: Triage & Fingerprinting
questions.description: Load the binary in a static analysis tool. Identify: (1) the target architecture and OS, (2) the compiler and approximate build date from PE header artifacts, (3) whether a packer or protector is present and which one. Submit the packer identification string as the flag.
questions.hint: Run FLOSS and Detect-It-Easy against the binary before opening it in a disassembler. Check the PE section names and entropy values — high entropy sections indicate packing.

questions.title: Unpack & Reconstruct Entry Point
questions.description: The binary is packed. Attach a debugger, let the unpacking stub execute until it reaches the original entry point (OEP), then dump the unpacked image. Load the dump into Ghidra and auto-analyze. Identify the first meaningful function called after entry — not a CRT or loader stub. Submit its virtual address as the flag.
questions.hint: Look for a jump to a region that was written at runtime. Set a hardware write breakpoint on the destination memory range, let it fire, then follow the final JMP to OEP.

questions.title: Persistence Mechanism
questions.description: The binary installs a persistence mechanism on first run. Using behavioral analysis (Process Monitor + sandbox trace), identify exactly how it achieves persistence: the registry key path, scheduled task name, or service entry it creates. Submit the persistence artifact name as the flag.
questions.hint: Filter Process Monitor for RegSetValue and CreateFile operations during the first 10 seconds of execution inside the sandbox VM.

questions.title: C2 Communication Protocol
questions.description: The binary beacons to a remote server. The destination is not hardcoded as a plain string — it is derived algorithmically at runtime. Reverse the domain generation algorithm (DGA) or decode the encrypted endpoint. Submit the decoded C2 address as the flag.
questions.hint: Look for base64 or XOR decoding routines near the networking calls (WSAConnect, InternetConnect, or WinHTTP functions). Emulate the decoding function in Python to recover the plaintext.

questions.title: Vulnerability — The Backdoor
questions.description: The binary contains a backdoor that allows the attacker to execute arbitrary commands on the host with SYSTEM privileges. Identify the exact vulnerability class (e.g., command injection, deserialization, memory corruption), the function name or offset where it occurs, and the trigger condition. Submit the function offset and vulnerability class as the flag.

faq.a: All activity takes place inside a fully isolated lab environment with no connection to the public internet. Participants operate exclusively on systems they are explicitly authorized to interact with. Applying any technique outside this environment is prohibited.

faq.q: What is the purpose of building a botnet here?
faq.a: Understanding offensive techniques in depth is one of the most effective paths to building strong defenses. Defensive teams will analyze every submission to extract detection logic, IOCs, and behavioral signatures they can use in real-world environments.

faq.q: What reference botnets can I study?
faq.a: Participants may study publicly documented botnets such as Mirai and Satori using published research papers, academic write-ups, and disclosed CVE analyses. Direct use of leaked source code is not permitted.

Referees and defensive teams evaluate each botnet on architecture quality, real-world fidelity, documentation, and the value of defensive insights it provides. Points are awarded for both offensive completeness and the quality of your own defensive write-up.

faq.q: What happens to submitted code after the event?
faq.a: All code remains within the competition environment and is never distributed publicly. It is used solely for defensive research by the organizing team.

lab.title: Lab Objectives
lab.subtitle: Isolated lab environment — no external network access
lab.description: Participants are challenged to develop and deploy a botnet inspired by existing botnets such as Mirai or Satori. The botnet should demonstrate key characteristics of real-world botnet architectures, including command-and-control (C2) communication, device management, and coordinated operations. Participants may use publicly disclosed CVEs to demonstrate how vulnerable systems can be compromised within the designated CTF environment. The objective is to understand how botnets are constructed and operate, providing defensive teams with a realistic adversarial scenario to investigate and defend against. Once development is complete, the submitted botnet will be examined by the referees and defensive teams, who will evaluate its behavior, architecture, and security implications.
lab.disclaimer: AUTHORIZED ENVIRONMENT ONLY. All botnet code, C2 infrastructure, and exploitation techniques must operate exclusively within the provided lab subnet (192.168.100.0/24). Any attempt to reach external networks, real infrastructure, or systems outside the lab range will result in immediate disqualification and may be referred to law enforcement. This environment is monitored at all times.

questions.title: C2 Server Implementation
questions.description: Design and implement a command-and-control server within the lab environment. It must support: (1) authenticated bot registration, (2) a tasking queue for distributing commands to connected bots, (3) status reporting from bots, and (4) an operator interface. Submit the C2 protocol specification as the flag.
questions.hint: Start with a simple TCP or HTTP-based protocol. Document every message type clearly — the defensive team will need to build detectors from your spec.

questions.title: Bot Client — Beacon & Execute
questions.description: Develop the bot agent that runs on compromised lab nodes. It must: beacon to the C2 server on a configurable interval, receive and execute commands, report results back, and maintain persistence across reboots on the lab target. Submit the beacon interval and persistence mechanism as the flag.
questions.hint: Keep the beacon protocol simple but document it thoroughly. Persistence options include cron jobs, systemd units, or rc.local — all valid within the lab.

questions.title: Propagation via Disclosed CVE
questions.description: Using a publicly disclosed CVE assigned to one of the intentionally vulnerable lab targets (see the lab CVE list), demonstrate how your bot could compromise a new host and add it to the botnet. The vulnerable targets are listed in /lab/targets.txt on the lab VM. Submit the CVE number and your exploitation approach as the flag.
questions.hint: Review the CVSS score and published PoC for each listed CVE. Choose one with a network-accessible attack vector. Use Metasploit or a custom exploit — both are permitted on the lab targets.

questions.title: Coordinated Operation
questions.description: Using your C2 and at least 3 compromised lab nodes, demonstrate a coordinated operation: a synchronized DDoS simulation against the lab's designated target server (192.168.100.254). The target server measures and logs incoming request volume. Submit the peak requests-per-second achieved as the flag.
questions.hint: Coordinate timing via your C2's tasking queue. HTTP flood is the simplest approach. The target server accepts connections on port 80 and logs all requests to /var/log/ddos-sim.log.

questions.title: Defensive Write-Up — IOCs & Detection Rules
questions.description: Analyze your own botnet from a defender's perspective and produce a defensive report covering: (1) a full list of IOCs (IPs, domains, file hashes, registry keys, process names), (2) at least 3 Sigma or Snort/Suricata detection rules targeting your botnet's behavior, and (3) recommended mitigations. The quality of this report is worth as many points as the technical challenges combined. Submit your report to the referee portal to receive the flag.
questions.hint: Think like a SOC analyst who has never seen your botnet before. What would they see in firewall logs, process monitors, and network captures? Write rules that catch your own traffic.

hero.headline: The Data Is There. Go Get It.
hero.description: ScrapeCTF is a web data extraction competition covering the full scraping stack: HTTP client engineering, HTML/JSON parsing, JavaScript-rendered SPA scraping, anti-bot bypass, API reverse engineering, and large-scale data pipeline assembly. All targets are purpose-built challenge servers — no real websites, no ToS violations, no grey areas. If it's on the challenge server, you're authorized to scrape it.

categories.description: Session management, cookie handling, custom headers, redirect chains, and authentication flows.

categories.description: Scraping React, Vue, and Angular apps that render entirely in the browser — Playwright and Puppeteer territory.

faq.a: No. All targets are purpose-built challenge servers hosted for this event. You are explicitly authorized to scrape them by any means necessary. No real websites, no ToS issues, no legal grey areas.
Any language. Python (httpx, requests, scrapy, Playwright, Selenium, parsel, BeautifulSoup) is the most common, but Node.js (Puppeteer, Cheerio), Go, and Rust scrapers are all valid.
Each challenge defines a flag extraction objective — scrape a specific data point from the target server and submit it in SCRAPE{...} format. The flag value is embedded in the data you extract.
Yes — two challenges require a real browser (Playwright or Puppeteer) because the targets render entirely in JavaScript. Headless browser automation is part of the skill set being tested.

faq.q: Can I use proxy pools or IP rotation?
faq.a: Yes. For anti-bot bypass challenges, rotating proxies and user-agent spoofing are explicitly permitted and expected. The lab provides a small proxy list for teams without their own.

lab.title: Scraping Challenges
lab.subtitle: All targets are live on the challenge server — start scraping
lab.description: Eight challenges in increasing difficulty. Each challenge defines a target URL and the data you need to extract. Flags are embedded in the extracted data. Static targets stay up for the full 36 hours; dynamic targets (rate-limited, bot-protected) reset every 6 hours.

questions.title: Static HTML — Product Catalog
questions.description: The target server hosts a paginated product catalog across 50 pages of static HTML. Scrape all product names, SKUs, and prices. The flag is the SHA-256 hash of all SKUs sorted alphabetically and joined with newlines. Pagination uses standard ?page=N query params.
questions.hint: Use requests + BeautifulSoup or httpx + parsel. Find the pagination range from the first page's nav element. Pool your requests with asyncio or a thread pool for speed.

questions.title: Authentication & Session Cookies
questions.description: The target has a login wall. Credentials are posted in the challenge description. After login, scrape the user dashboard which contains a hidden data table not visible to logged-out visitors. The flag is in a table cell with class 'secret-value'.
questions.hint: Use a requests.Session() to persist cookies across the login POST and subsequent GETs. Check the login form for CSRF tokens — they need to be submitted with the credentials.

questions.title: JavaScript-Rendered SPA
questions.description: The target is a React single-page application. The HTML returned by the server is an empty shell — all content is loaded via API calls after the JS executes. Scrape the full article list from the rendered DOM. The flag is embedded in the last article's body text.
questions.hint: Use Playwright: `page.goto(url)` then `page.wait_for_selector('.article-list')` before extracting. Alternatively, open DevTools Network tab on the target manually to find the underlying API call and hit it directly.

questions.title: Undocumented REST API
questions.description: A mobile app's backend API is running on the challenge server. No documentation exists. Intercept the app's traffic (a web simulation is provided), reverse engineer the authentication scheme (HMAC-signed requests), and extract the full user list from the /api/users endpoint. The flag is the email address of user ID 1337.
questions.hint: Open the web simulation in DevTools and watch the Network tab. Look for Authorization headers on API requests — they usually follow a pattern like HMAC-SHA256(timestamp + path + body, secret_key). Find the secret key in the JS source.

questions.title: Rate-Limited Endpoint
questions.description: The target endpoint returns one record per request and allows a maximum of 10 requests per minute per IP. You need to collect 500 records. Implement a compliant scraper that respects the rate limit and collects all records within the competition window. The flag is embedded in record #499.
questions.hint: Use a token bucket or simple sleep-based rate limiter. 500 records at 10/min = 50 minutes — well within the window. Store results to disk as you go in case of crashes.

questions.title: Anti-Bot: Fingerprinting & Behavioral Detection
questions.description: The target runs a Cloudflare-style JS challenge and behavioral analysis — it blocks headless browsers detected by missing browser properties, unusual TLS fingerprints, or non-human interaction timing. Bypass the detection and scrape the protected data table. The flag is in the 7th row.
questions.hint: Use Playwright with stealth patches (playwright-stealth or puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth). Randomize mouse movements and scroll before clicking. Check if the TLS fingerprint (JA3) is being filtered — use a residential proxy if so.

questions.title: GraphQL Introspection & Data Extraction
questions.description: The target exposes a GraphQL API with introspection enabled. Enumerate the full schema, identify the query that returns flagged data, and extract it. The API uses cursor-based pagination — scrape all pages. The flag is in the notes field of the last node.
questions.hint: Run a full introspection query first: `{ __schema { types { name fields { name } } } }`. Use a tool like GraphQL Voyager or Altair to visualize the schema. Then write a paginated query using the `after` cursor field.

questions.title: Full Pipeline — Scrape, Clean, Aggregate
questions.description: Three separate target servers each host one piece of a dataset: product catalog, inventory levels, and pricing history. Scrape all three, join them on a shared product_id field, clean the data (normalize dates, deduplicate entries, fill missing values), and compute the total inventory value across all products. Submit the total as the flag.
questions.hint: Tackle each source separately first. Use pandas for the join and aggregation. Watch for inconsistent product_id formats between sources (some use int, some use zero-padded strings) — normalize before joining.

hero.headline: Write It. Understand It. Build Defenses That Stop It.

By constructing and studying these threats firsthand, participants develop a deep, practitioner-level understanding of how malware operates, evades detection, and persists. Every offensive challenge is paired with a defensive analysis requirement, ensuring participants leave equipped to defend real systems against the threats they studied.

Deploying, distributing, or using any code or technique from this competition against systems you do not own and are not explicitly authorized to test is illegal under computer crime laws in most jurisdictions. By participating, you agree to these terms unconditionally. The organizing team reserves the right to disqualify and report participants who violate these terms.

faq.q: Why does this CTF involve writing malware?
faq.a: The most effective malware defenders are those who have built and analyzed real malware themselves. This competition creates a legal, controlled environment where that knowledge is built responsibly. Every challenge has a mandatory defensive analysis component — you are not done until you have documented how to detect what you built.

Yes — within the authorized lab environment. Participants operate exclusively on systems they are authorized to use, with no access to real networks or third-party systems. The legal boundary is clear: everything inside the lab is authorized; everything outside is not.

faq.q: What malware archetypes are in scope?
faq.a: Trojans and droppers, worms (simulated propagation only), ransomware (encryption logic only — no real ransom, no real victims), rootkits (userland only unless a kernel lab is specified), and evasion-focused loaders. Destructive payloads, data exfiltration to external systems, and anything targeting real infrastructure are explicitly out of scope.

faq.q: What happens to malware samples after the event?
faq.a: All samples remain inside the lab environment and are submitted to the organizing team for defensive research only. Samples are never published or redistributed. Participants may not retain copies outside the lab.

faq.q: What if I accidentally break out of the sandbox?
faq.a: Immediately stop what you are doing and report it to the event organizers via the emergency contact in your participant pack. Do not attempt to continue or cover it up. We have monitoring in place and will treat transparent reports as accidents, not violations.

lab.title: Malware Lab Challenges
lab.subtitle: Sandboxed, isolated, and monitored — Windows & Linux targets
lab.description: Each challenge below operates in a fully isolated sandbox with no external network access. You will develop malware archetypes, run them against lab targets, analyze their behavior, and produce a defensive write-up. Flags are revealed when the technical objective is met. The defensive write-up for each challenge is mandatory and worth 50% of the challenge's total points.
lab.disclaimer: AUTHORIZED LAB ONLY — MONITORED AT ALL TIMES. All code must run exclusively inside the lab VM. No sample, tool, or technique from this competition may be used outside the authorized environment. Destructive payloads, real ransomware key infrastructure, and any action targeting systems outside the lab subnet are strictly prohibited and will result in immediate disqualification and referral to relevant authorities.

questions.title: Trojan Dropper
questions.description: Create a Windows executable that appears to be a legitimate utility (e.g., a fake PDF viewer or system cleaner). When run, it silently drops and executes a secondary payload (a benign calculator binary provided by the lab). The dropper must bypass Windows SmartScreen in the lab environment. Submit the dropper's disguise technique and evasion method as the flag.
questions.hint: Embedding the payload as a resource and using a legitimate-looking icon and version info are common first steps. For SmartScreen, consider code signing with the lab's test certificate or catalog-based bypass.

questions.title: Worm — Simulated Propagation
questions.description: Develop a worm that, once running on lab-host-01, automatically spreads to lab-host-02 and lab-host-03 using either a disclosed vulnerability (CVE listed in /lab/worm-targets.txt) or a simulated credential reuse attack using the lab's credential list. The worm must leave a marker file on each host it compromises. Submit the propagation method and marker file path as the flag.
questions.hint: SMB credential reuse is a classic worm vector and straightforward to implement. Use the lab's provided credential list (admin:labpass123). Alternatively, the lab targets run a vulnerable service listed in worm-targets.txt.

questions.title: Ransomware — Encryption Pattern
questions.description: Implement the encryption logic used by ransomware: generate a session key, encrypt a directory of test files using AES-256, store the encrypted key (simulated as written to a local file — no real key server), and produce a ransom note. The lab provides a directory of dummy files to encrypt. Submit the encryption scheme and key storage method as the flag. No real ransom infrastructure, no victim contact — this is encryption logic only.
questions.hint: Use AES-256 in CBC mode for file encryption and RSA-2048 to wrap the session key. The lab provides a test RSA key pair. Write the encrypted session key to encrypted_key.bin in the target directory.

questions.title: Persistence — Three Mechanisms
questions.description: Demonstrate three distinct persistence mechanisms on the Windows lab target, each surviving a full system reboot: (1) a registry run key, (2) a scheduled task, and (3) a Windows service. Each must execute a benign ping command on startup. Submit the name, path, and trigger of each mechanism as the flag.
questions.hint: Use sc.exe or the Windows Service API for the service. For the scheduled task, schtasks /create is the simplest path. Document the exact registry key path for the run key — defenders will need this to write detection rules.

questions.title: AV Evasion — Bypass Signature Detection
questions.description: Take the dropper from Challenge 1 and modify it to bypass the AV engine running on the lab's isolated test VM (ClamAV + a commercial AV in the lab). The objective is not to 'win against AV' — it is to understand which evasion techniques trigger alerts and which do not. Document every technique you tried and its outcome. Submit the final evasion method and your detection bypass rate as the flag.
questions.hint: Start by submitting the original binary to understand which signatures fire. Then try: string obfuscation, packing with UPX, XOR-encoding the payload, and sleep-based sandbox evasion. Document each result — the write-up is half the points.

questions.title: Incident Response — Full Analysis Report
questions.description: A pre-built malware sample (sample_unknown.exe) is provided in /lab/ir/. Perform a complete analysis: static (strings, imports, sections, packer), dynamic (API trace, file/registry/network activity), and behavioral (what does it ultimately do?). Produce an incident report with: a full IOC list, a kill chain diagram, three detection rules (Sigma or Yara), and recommended remediation steps. Submit your report to the referee portal to receive the flag.
questions.hint: Start with FLOSS for strings, then PEStudio for static analysis. Use Process Monitor and Wireshark in the sandbox for dynamic analysis. The sample is packed — use x64dbg to dump it at OEP before deep static analysis.

allowed: Develop and run all malware samples exclusively inside the provided sandbox VMs
Implement encryption, dropper, persistence, and evasion logic for educational purposes
Use any tool available in the lab (Ghidra, x64dbg, Python, Metasploit, ClamAV, etc.)

Collaborate with your registered team members within your isolated lab segment

Submit any sample to public malware analysis platforms (VirusTotal, Any.run) during the competition

hero.headline: Reverse the App. Break the Pinning. Own the Device.
hero.description: Mobile applications are among the most underaudited attack surfaces in modern security. MobileCTF covers the full Android and iOS security testing lifecycle: static APK and IPA analysis, runtime manipulation with Frida, SSL pinning bypass, insecure storage exploitation, and mobile malware triage. All challenges run on provided emulators and test devices in the lab — no personal devices required.

categories.name: Certificate Pinning

categories.name: API & Backend

faq.q: Do I need a physical Android or iOS device?
faq.a: No. All challenges run on Android emulators (provided via the lab VM) and an iOS simulator. A rooted Android AVD is pre-configured with Frida server already running.

jadx and apktool for static analysis, Frida and objection for runtime hooks, Burp Suite for traffic interception, MobSF for quick automated scanning, and adb for device interaction. All are pre-installed in the lab VM.

faq.q: Do I need to know Java or Kotlin for Android challenges?
faq.a: Reading decompiled Java/Kotlin helps but is not required for all challenges. Many flags can be extracted by pattern-matching strings, analyzing smali bytecode, or hooking at the right method without reading every line.

Yes — two challenges target iOS IPAs and use the provided iOS simulator. These focus on static analysis (class-dump, strings, plist inspection) rather than runtime exploitation, since iOS runtime hooking requires a jailbroken device.
Flags are in MOB{...} format. They are embedded in the app binary, returned by the backend API once exploited, or printed by a Frida hook when the correct condition is met.

lab.title: Mobile Challenges
lab.subtitle: Android emulator + iOS simulator — lab VM required
lab.description: Eight challenges across Android and iOS. Static challenges can be solved without running the app; dynamic challenges require the lab emulator. All APKs and IPAs are purpose-built for this event. Flags are in MOB{...} format.

questions.title: Hardcoded Secrets — Android (static)
questions.description: An Android APK (vault_app.apk) is provided. Decompile it with jadx. The app validates a PIN before granting access. Find the hardcoded PIN or the validation logic and extract the flag without running the app.
questions.hint: Open the decompiled source in jadx-gui. Search for string comparisons involving 'pin', 'password', or 'secret'. The flag may be in a string resource file (res/values/strings.xml) rather than Java code.

questions.title: Insecure SharedPreferences
questions.description: Install login_app.apk on the lab emulator. Log in with the test account (user: guest, pass: guest123). The app stores session data insecurely after login. Pull the data directory from the emulator and find the flag stored in plaintext.
questions.hint: Use `adb shell` to navigate to /data/data/<package_name>/shared_prefs/. Pull the XML files with `adb pull`. Look for any value that looks like a token, key, or flag.

questions.title: SQLite Database Extraction
questions.description: notes_app.apk stores user notes in a local SQLite database. Install the app, create a few notes, then extract and query the database. One note contains the flag — it was inserted by the app itself on first launch and is not visible in the UI.
questions.hint: Pull /data/data/<package_name>/databases/ with adb. Open the .db file with sqlite3 or DB Browser for SQLite. Run `SELECT * FROM notes;` and check all rows, including those with a hidden or archived flag.

questions.title: SSL Pinning Bypass
questions.description: secure_api.apk communicates with a backend API over HTTPS with certificate pinning enabled — it rejects Burp Suite's proxy certificate. Use Frida and the objection toolkit to bypass the pinning at runtime, then intercept the app's traffic in Burp. The flag is returned by the /api/secret endpoint when called with a valid session token.
questions.hint: Start the app with `objection -g <package> explore`, then run `android sslpinning disable`. If that fails, use a custom Frida script to hook TrustManager.checkServerTrusted() and OkHttp's CertificatePinner. Set Burp as the system proxy in the emulator's WiFi settings.

questions.title: Frida Hook — Authentication Bypass
questions.description: admin_app.apk has an admin panel that is only accessible to users with isAdmin == true. This value is set server-side and cannot be changed in the UI. Write a Frida script that hooks the method responsible for checking admin status and forces it to return true. The flag is displayed in the admin panel once accessed.
questions.hint: Decompile the APK first to find the method name that checks admin status (look for methods returning boolean near 'admin' or 'role'). Then use Frida to hook it: `Java.use('com.example.app.AuthManager').isAdmin.implementation = function() { return true; }`

questions.title: Obfuscated APK — Deobfuscate & Extract
questions.description: obfuscated_app.apk has been processed with ProGuard — class names, method names, and string constants are obfuscated. The app validates a license key using a multi-step algorithm. Deobfuscate the relevant logic, understand the key derivation, and extract or calculate the valid license key. The flag is revealed when the correct key is entered.
questions.hint: Start by renaming obfuscated classes based on what they do, not what they're called. Look for the class that handles button click events on the license screen. String obfuscation is often done with a simple XOR or base64 — look for static initializers that decode values at runtime.

questions.title: Mobile Malware Triage — Suspicious APK
questions.description: malware_sample.apk was flagged by a user who downloaded it from a third-party app store. Analyze it statically and dynamically. Identify: (1) all dangerous permissions it requests and their purpose, (2) any hidden payload or second-stage download, (3) the C2 endpoint it contacts, and (4) the data it exfiltrates. Submit the C2 address and exfiltrated data type as the flag.
questions.hint: Start with MobSF for an automated overview, then dig into the decompiled source manually. Look for BroadcastReceivers triggered on BOOT_COMPLETED, background Services, and any network calls to hardcoded IPs. Run it in the emulator with network traffic captured in Wireshark.

questions.title: iOS IPA Analysis — Hidden API Key
questions.description: A compiled iOS IPA (tracker_app.ipa) is provided. Extract the IPA, inspect the binary and bundle resources. The app contains a hardcoded API key used to authenticate with a tracking backend. Find the key — it is not in plaintext but is reconstructed from fragments at runtime. Submit the full reconstructed API key as the flag.
questions.hint: Unzip the IPA and inspect the app bundle. Use `strings` on the Mach-O binary and search for base64 fragments. Use class-dump or ipsw to list Objective-C classes and methods. The key may be split across multiple string literals concatenated in a +load or viewDidLoad method.

lab.title: RE Challenges
lab.subtitle: Binaries and firmware targets
lab.description: Analyze the provided targets and extract the hidden flag from each. Work inside the lab VM — do not run unknown binaries on your host machine. Flags are in RE{...} format.

questions.title: intro_x64
questions.description: A stripped ELF x64 binary. It accepts a string argument and prints 'Correct!' if the input matches the expected value. Find the expected string and submit the flag.
questions.hint: Open in Ghidra. Find main(), follow the string comparison, and read off the expected bytes.

questions.title: vm_check

questions.hint: Use binwalk to extract the firmware. The flag is not in plaintext — check config files and compiled binaries inside.

questions.title: mystery.pcap + decoder

hero.headline: Find What No One Has Found Before.
hero.description: Zero-day research is the frontier of offensive security — discovering vulnerabilities that exist in software before any vendor, researcher, or attacker has publicly identified them. This CTF provides a controlled, legally authorized environment to practice the full zero-day research lifecycle: systematic vulnerability discovery, root-cause analysis, exploit development, and responsible coordinated disclosure. All targets are purpose-built or provided explicitly for this event. The goal is to build researchers who find bugs to fix them, not to weaponize them.
hero.disclaimer: FOR AUTHORIZED RESEARCH ONLY. All vulnerability research, fuzzing, and exploit development must be conducted exclusively against the designated lab targets. Applying these techniques against real software, systems, or infrastructure you do not own and are not authorized to test is illegal under computer fraud and abuse laws worldwide. Any real zero-day vulnerabilities discovered — in lab targets or otherwise — must be reported through responsible disclosure, not sold, withheld, or weaponized. By participating, you agree to these terms unconditionally.

categories.name: Vulnerability Research

categories.description: Automated vulnerability discovery using coverage-guided fuzzers like AFL++ and libFuzzer.

categories.name: Memory Corruption
categories.description: Stack and heap buffer overflows, use-after-free, type confusion, and out-of-bounds read/write.

categories.name: Logic & Auth Flaws
categories.description: Authentication bypass, race conditions, integer overflows, and business logic vulnerabilities.

categories.name: Exploit Development
categories.description: Turn a confirmed bug into a reliable, weaponizable proof-of-concept under modern mitigations (ASLR, NX, CFG).

categories.name: Responsible Disclosure
categories.description: Write a complete CVE-style vulnerability report and walk through the coordinated disclosure process.

faq.q: What makes this different from a regular pwn CTF?
faq.a: Standard pwn challenges hand you a known vulnerability and ask you to exploit it. This CTF asks you to find the vulnerability first — the bug is unknown, undocumented, and unreported. You are doing real zero-day research on purpose-built targets.

Targets are purpose-built binaries and services designed to contain realistic vulnerability classes. Some targets are inspired by real CVEs in structure but are not the actual vulnerable software. Source code is provided for some targets; others are black-box.

faq.q: What if I find a real zero-day in real software during the event?
faq.a: Report it to the organizers immediately. We will help you go through coordinated disclosure with the vendor. Under no circumstances should you exploit, sell, or publicly disclose a real vulnerability without following responsible disclosure first.

faq.q: What mitigations are enabled on targets?
faq.a: Targets run with realistic modern mitigations: ASLR, NX/DEP, stack canaries, and PIE are enabled by default. Some challenges disable specific mitigations as the vulnerability class requires — this is documented per-challenge.

This varies by jurisdiction and is a legally complex area. For this competition: all discovered vulnerabilities in lab targets are competition property. Techniques learned here must not be used to discover, develop, or sell exploits against real systems outside the authorized lab.

lab.title: Research Targets
lab.subtitle: Black-box and white-box — fuzzing and manual audit
lab.description: Six targets are provided in increasing difficulty. For each: find at least one exploitable vulnerability, demonstrate it with a working proof-of-concept, and submit a disclosure-quality write-up. Flags are revealed when your PoC achieves the stated impact (e.g., arbitrary code execution, authentication bypass, or memory leak). The disclosure report is mandatory and weighted equally with the technical exploit.
lab.disclaimer: AUTHORIZED TARGETS ONLY — ALL ACTIVITY IS LOGGED. All fuzzing, debugging, and exploitation must target only the binaries and services listed below, running inside the lab VM. Do not scan, probe, or fuzz any host outside the lab environment. Real zero-day techniques carry serious legal weight — you are practicing them here under explicit authorization. Using anything you learn here against unauthorized systems is a criminal offense.

questions.title: Fuzz & Crash — target01 (white-box)
questions.description: Source code for target01 (a simple file parser) is provided in /lab/target01/. Set up AFL++ with coverage instrumentation, fuzz the parser, and produce at least one unique crash. Classify the crash: determine whether it is exploitable (write-what-where, control of RIP, or info leak). Submit the crash input and exploitability classification as the flag.
questions.hint: Compile with afl-cc -fsanitize=address for best crash visibility. Start with a small corpus of valid input files. Use afl-tmin to minimize the crashing input before analysis.

questions.title: Root Cause Analysis — provided crash
questions.description: A pre-generated crash (core dump + reproducer) for target02 is provided in /lab/target02/. Without source code, determine: (1) the exact vulnerable code path, (2) the vulnerability class (BOF, UAF, integer overflow, etc.), (3) which mitigations are bypassable, and (4) the minimum primitives available to an attacker. Submit the vulnerability class and exploitable primitive as the flag.
questions.hint: Open the core dump in GDB with PEDA or pwndbg. Run `bt` for the backtrace. Use `info registers` to see what an attacker controls at the crash point. Cross-reference with the binary in Ghidra.

questions.title: Stack Exploitation — target03 (ASLR + NX, no canary)
questions.description: target03 is a network service with a classic stack buffer overflow. ASLR and NX are enabled; stack canaries are disabled. Develop a working ROP chain that achieves arbitrary code execution (spawn /bin/sh on the lab host). Submit the working exploit script and the shell session proof as the flag.
questions.hint: Use ROPgadget or ropper to build your chain. The binary is not PIE — base addresses are static. Leak a libc address via a puts() call to defeat ASLR, then ret2libc. Use pwntools for socket interaction.

questions.title: Heap Exploitation — target04 (full mitigations)
questions.description: target04 is a binary with a use-after-free vulnerability. All mitigations are enabled: ASLR, NX, PIE, and stack canaries. Exploit the UAF to achieve arbitrary read/write, leak a heap and libc address, and gain code execution. Submit your exploit and the achieved impact as the flag.
questions.hint: Trigger the UAF by freeing an object and then reallocating it with a different type (type confusion). Use the resulting controlled read to leak a libc pointer from the freed chunk's fd/bk fields. House of Force or tcache poisoning are common next steps.

questions.title: Logic Flaw — authentication bypass in target05 web app
questions.description: target05 is a black-box web application running on the lab host at port 8080. It has a JWT-based login and an admin panel. No source code is provided. Find and exploit a logic or authentication flaw to access the admin panel without valid credentials. The flag is displayed in the admin panel once accessed.
questions.hint: Start with common JWT weaknesses: algorithm confusion (HS256 vs RS256), the 'none' algorithm, weak secret brute-force, and claim validation bypass. Also check for path traversal or IDOR to the admin endpoints.

questions.title: Full Chain + Disclosure Report
questions.description: Combine a vulnerability from target03 or target04 with the authentication bypass from target05 into a full exploit chain that achieves remote code execution starting from zero authentication. Then write a complete CVE-style disclosure report covering: vulnerability description, affected component, CVSS score with justification, proof-of-concept steps, root cause, and recommended fix. Submit both the chain PoC and the report to the referee portal.
